title: what your prayer is actually saying
hook: seven verses said in every prayer, many times a day, and what they actually say
carry: a conversation, answered line by line

segments.voice: Yesterday: bismillah, in the name of God. Today, the prayer that opens with it.

It's said in every unit of every prayer: seventeen times on an ordinary day. Many Muslims learned it by heart as children and could say it half asleep. Ask what it means, line by line, and a lot of people go quiet. There's a question people really ask: what's the point of praying in Arabic if I don't understand it? Today, the whole thing, in plain English.
screen: `SEVENTEEN TIMES A DAY.` → `WHAT DOES IT SAY?` → `IN PLAIN ENGLISH.`

segments.voice: It's called al-Fatiha, the opening: the first surah of the Qur'an, from a root meaning to open. A key, in Arabic, is a miftah. Seven short verses. Here they are, in plain words. In the name of God, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds. The Beneficent, the Merciful. Owner of the Day of Judgment. You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. Show us the straight path: the path of those You have favored, not of those who earn anger, nor of those who go astray. That's all of it. Notice the shape. It opens in yesterday's name. Then praise, and mercy said twice. Then it turns from talking about God to talking to God: You. And when it finally asks for something, it asks for one thing. Not money, not health. Directions. A saying the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reported from God describes it as a conversation. When someone praying says, praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds, God answers: My servant has praised Me. Line after line, an answer comes back. So here's the answer to the Arabic question. The words don't change. Knowing them changes how you say them. Even one line, known while you say it, gives a wandering mind somewhere to stand.
screen: `AL-FATIHA — THE OPENING.` · `SEVEN VERSES, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN ONE REQUEST.` · `A CONVERSATION, ANSWERED.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. On the way out, say the one request, in Arabic or in English: ihdina s-sirat al-mustaqim. Show us the straight path. It's the line the whole prayer leans toward.
Al-Fatiha. The opening: seven verses, praise first, then one request. Second word on your strand.
Your line: a conversation, answered line by line. Next time you hear it, you'll know what's being said. Day two, done.

screen: `DAY 2 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WATER BEFORE THE WORDS.`

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and at many other moments: over the sick, at a wedding, for someone who has died. Many learn it as children, before any other surah.

myth: al-Fatiha is mostly a list of requests
it's mostly praise. it asks for one thing: show us the straight path.
al-Fatiha is said in every unit of every prayer
a saying of the Prophet ﷺ says there is no prayer without it.

fork.setup: someone new to the prayer knows very little Arabic yet. which part does a saying of the Prophet ﷺ say no prayer can be without?
fork.reveal: there is no prayer without al-Fatiha. that's why it's usually among the first things a learner memorizes.

original.note: Arabic: "the opening." from f-t-h, to open, the same root as miftah, a key.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first chapter, recited from memory.
what it means: the opening — seven verses of praise and one request, said in every unit of every prayer.

what a scholar hears: a hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim divides it between God and the servant, verse by verse; the Qur'an's "seven oft-repeated" (15:87) is widely read as al-Fatiha; verse counts differ on whether the bismillah is its first verse.

story.title: the chief and the scorpion
story.text: A band of travelers asks a tribe for hospitality and is turned away. That night the tribe's chief is stung by a scorpion, nothing they try helps, and his people come to the very strangers they refused. One of the travelers sits by him and recites al-Fatiha over him, and the chief gets up as if he'd been untied. Back in Medina, the Prophet ﷺ asks the man: how did you know it's a healing?

wrong.myth: al-Fatiha is mostly asking God for things.
wrong.truth: it's mostly praise. it asks for one thing only: show us the straight path.

build.prompt: put the prayer's shape in order.

think.setup: a friend says: what's the point of praying in Arabic if I don't understand it? what's a good first step?
options: stop praying until you're fluent in Arabic.
learn what the seven verses say, a line at a time.
keep reciting; the meaning doesn't matter.
think.reveal: the words don't change. knowing them changes how you say them, and it's only seven lines.

notes: Moved: old day 6 (al-Fatiha, verse one) → day 2, rewritten from the audience research's #1 question ('what's the point of praying in Arabic if I don't understand it?'): the whole surah in plain English, its shape, and the conversation hadith. The verse-by-verse walk now runs days 12–16, and calls back to this day.

The seven verses are given in the app's own plain English, not quoted from Pickthall (sources: paraphrase). The count follows the Kufan numbering most printed copies use, with the bismillah as 1:1. Other counts don't number the bismillah and split verse 7; the surah has seven verses either way. A Keeper may want one sentence on this later.
'Seventeen times on an ordinary day': the seventeen required units (2+4+4+3+4); travelers who shorten prayers recite fewer. Kept from the earlier script; confirm under the claims rule.
Sahih Muslim 395 (the hadith qudsi, 'I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant') paraphrased; the script says 'a saying the Prophet reported from God'. Confirm.
Hadith numbers Bukhari 756 / Muslim 394 cited from memory; please confirm. The Hanafi school treats reciting al-Fatiha as required (wajib) rather than a pillar; the fork only reports the hadith.

Story card: the ruqya of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (Bukhari 5749, 2276; Muslim 2201), paraphrased; the sheep they were given is left out. 'As if he'd been untied' follows the hadith's image of a camel released from its hobble. Confirm the numbers and the retelling.

Reddit research (docs/learning/research-extra/REDDIT.md): the Arabic gap is also about staying present ('how do I stay focused?', 'what do I think about during long prayers?'). The teach's last line and the practice answer it gently (one line, known while you say it); no ruling on praying in other languages is given.
howItsDone mentions al-Fatiha recited over the sick, at weddings and for the dead: common practice in many communities, not universal. Confirm.
